title: Beads of prayer
hook: counting prayers on beads grew in the middle ages; the Orthodox use knotted prayer ropes

segments.voice: Yesterday, pilgrims' roads to Rome, Santiago and Canterbury, where the walking itself became prayer. Your line was the road is the prayer.

A grandmother's hands rest in her lap, a loop of beads running through her fingers. Her lips move. Every few seconds, her thumb slides one bead along. In another house, in another church, a monk holds a loop of black wool tied in thick knots, and his thumb moves the same way. Bead, word. Knot, word. Neither of them is looking at their hands. The hands keep count so the heart doesn't have to.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN HER FINGERS.`

segments.voice: Counting prayers is an old Christian habit. Tradition remembers desert monks who counted their prayers with pebbles, moving one stone from one pile to another. Later, in the West, people threaded beads on a string to count the Lord's Prayer, the Our Father, again and again. In the middle ages these strings grew into the rosary, where Catholics pray the Hail Mary in sets, each set beginning with the Our Father, while they think about scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary. In the East, Orthodox monks use a prayer rope, a loop of knotted wool, and with each knot they say the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. They tell a story about it. A holy monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept untying them, so the monk learned to tie each knot as a little web of crosses, and the devil couldn't undo them. Whatever its origin, the story says something true about these ropes: each knot is made to hold. Why repeat a prayer at all? Paul tells one church, in the King James Bible, "Pray without ceasing." Repetition is one way people have tried to obey that line. But Jesus also says, in Matthew, "use not vain repetitions." For that reason some Protestants are cautious about counted prayers, and pray in their own words. Catholic and Orthodox teachers answer that a prayer said from the heart isn't vain, however often it's said. Each side reads the same Gospel seriously.
screen: `BEADS FOR THE OUR FATHER, THEN THE ROSARY.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap and choose one short line: the Jesus Prayer, the first line of the Our Father, a line from a Psalm, or, if you don't pray, a single word like thanks, or the name of someone you love. Touch your thumb to one fingertip and say the line slowly, then the next fingertip, ten times across both hands. If you lose count, start again without fuss.
Jesus Prayer. The words Orthodox monks repeat on a knotted prayer rope, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, so the hands keep count and the heart can pray.
Your line: counting love. Your own ten fingers can make a simple prayer rope. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary on a string of beads, alone or together, and Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope; some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too.

chat.says: What's the Jesus Prayer? Is it the same as the Our Father?
options: No. It's one short line, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, said on a prayer rope.
Yes. It's another name for the Our Father, the prayer Jesus taught his followers.
It's the rosary's main prayer, the Hail Mary, said in sets on a string of beads.
chat.meaning: The Jesus Prayer is the short line Orthodox monks repeat on each knot of a prayer rope: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.

notes: Claims rule: no counts (number of beads, knots or Hail Marys) or dates are given. Protestant caution is phrased as 'some Protestants'.
Desert monk counting prayers with pebbles: Palladius, Lausiac History (Paul of Pherme); given as 'tradition remembers'. Confirm.
Paternoster beads in the West, growth of the rosary in the middle ages: standard; confirm summary.
Prayer rope legend (often attributed to Pachomius): labeled a story, not a record. Confirm.
Jesus Prayer quoted in its common form (a traditional prayer, not a new one).

Matthew 6:7 quoted only in part ('use not vain repetitions'); the full verse continues 'as the heathen do', omitted to avoid a contrast with another tradition. Confirm the omission is fair to the text.
